summary: Ignis Atlas is an interactive, source-linked dashboard for NASA microgravity combustion research. It indexes 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations, presents 14 curated findings, and summarizes experimental tables from BASS-II, FLEX, and SAME. Users filter by fire-safety task, inspect transparent relevance scores and original NASA links, and generate a cited evidence brief that keeps observations separate from interpretations and limits. It addresses Flame in Freefall by making prevention, detection, suppression, and flame-physics research easier to find and compare for crewed-habitat planning. Rankings are editorial reading priorities, not hazard predictions. Moon and Mars views warn that microgravity data do not validate partial-gravity outcomes. OpenAI Codex assisted with code and evidence curation; the in-app brief uses deterministic retrieval, not a live generative model.
details:
Ignis Atlas organizes NASA microgravity combustion research for crewed-habitat fire-safety study. It indexes 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations and 14 curated findings. Users filter by prevention, smoke detection, suppression, or flame physics; search experiment text; open original NASA records; and inspect linked tables and publications. Each finding keeps its reported observation, test conditions, interpretation, safety question, scope limit, and source link together. A deterministic brief builder retrieves matching findings and creates a cited summary. The ledger and brief can be exported.

Three descriptive snapshots come from original NASA PSI CSV tables. BASS-II has 129 test rows and calibrated initial oxygen values of 13.6–22.2% by volume. FLEX has 274 rows with literal test-end labels of 186 Extinction, 61 Disruption, and 27 Completion. SAME has eight sample rows; only four explicitly state numeric airflow values (5–10 cm/s). Missing values were not imputed. These counts and ranges are not fire-risk probabilities or universal material thresholds.

The transparent ranking combines curated focus tags, text overlap, linked findings, table availability, publication count, and whether the challenge names an investigation. Its point breakdown is a reading priority, not a hazard or quality grade. Mission context changes the caution text, not the score. The tool does not predict ignition or extinction in an untested habitat or certify hardware. NASA microgravity results do not validate lunar or Martian partial-gravity fire behavior.

The app uses static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Python standard-library scripts captured NASA PSI metadata and CSV snapshots. Full source and data are linked in the site footer under Apache 2.0. OpenAI Codex assisted with the initial solution design, code, evidence curation, writing, and demo. The participant selected the Flame in Freefall challenge and requested the build. The site visibly discloses AI assistance and cites original NASA sources.
